title: NCLAT: 2026 IBC Change Removing Guarantors' Interim Moratorium Applies To Pending Cases Too
seo_title: NCLAT: Guarantor Moratorium Change Hits Old Cases
meta_description: NCLAT holds the 2026 IBC amendment excluding personal guarantors from interim moratorium under Section 96 applies retroactively to pending applications.
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi
bench: Justice Mohammad Faiz Alam Khan (Judicial Member) and Naresh Salecha (Technical Member)
case_name: Sangeeta Aggarwal & Ors. v. Equentia Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
body: Three personal guarantors who thought they had bought themselves protection by invoking an interim moratorium have found the ground shifting under them, courtesy of a mid-year change to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code that Parliament made expressly to stop guarantors from doing exactly what these three tried. The NCLAT's Principal Bench in New Delhi has now confirmed that the change reaches back to catch applications that were already pending when it came into force.

The appellants, Sangeeta Aggarwal, Saloni Ayush Aggarwal and Sri Narayan Aggarwal, had stood as personal guarantors for a financial facility that Equentia Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. extended to Prafful Overseas Private Limited. Equentia moved an application under Section 95 of the IBC against the three guarantors on 5 November 2025. According to the record before the Tribunal, this was done while an interim moratorium triggered by an earlier Section 95 application from Canara Bank, against the same guarantors, was still subsisting under the unamended Section 96.

At the time, Section 96 gave a personal guarantor an automatic interim moratorium the moment any application under Section 95 was filed against them, shielding them from parallel recovery action while that application was pending. Guarantors facing recovery from multiple lenders learned to treat the filing of one Section 95 application, even one that might later be withdrawn or dismissed, as a shield against every other creditor trying to move against them at the same time. That is the pattern a Parliamentary Select Committee examining the IBC Amendment Bill, 2025 flagged as a misuse of the moratorium provision, intended to protect a guarantor's assets for an orderly resolution process, rather than as a tool to stall legitimate recovery indefinitely.

Parliament responded by inserting Section 96(4), effective from 26 May 2026, carving personal guarantors to corporate debtors out of the interim moratorium regime altogether. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India followed up with a circular dated 21 September 2026, clarifying that the interim moratorium under Section 96 had ceased to operate from that date even for applications that were already pending when the amendment took effect.

Before the NCLAT, the Aggarwals argued that this reasoning could not save Equentia's application, because it had been filed in November 2025, months before Section 96(4) existed, at a time when the Canara Bank moratorium was still in force and barred any parallel Section 95 proceeding. Their position was that an application void for want of protection at the time it was filed could not be revived by a later amendment never meant to operate backward on an already-defective filing.

The Tribunal rejected that argument. It held that Section 96(4) operates retroactively and reaches pending proceedings, including ones filed before the amendment existed, so long as they remained undecided when the amendment came into force. The Bench reasoned that a guarantor enjoying the interim moratorium in a pending application had no vested right in that protection capable of resisting the amendment's retroactive sweep, since the moratorium was always a creature of statute rather than a substantive right earned by the guarantor.

NCLT New Delhi had reached a similar conclusion in an earlier, related ruling on the same point, and the Bombay High Court and Delhi High Court have each upheld the same retroactive reading in separate proceedings through 2026, so this NCLAT order adds to what is now a fairly consistent line of authority across forums rather than breaking new ground on the legal question itself. What makes it notable is that it applies that settled position to an application that predates the amendment by several months, closing off the argument that only applications filed on or after 26 May 2026 can rely on Section 96(4).

For promoters and family businesses who have given personal guarantees for company borrowings, many of whom treated an existing Section 95 filing by one lender as cover against the rest, the practical message is that this shield no longer holds, whatever the date the original application happened to be filed. Lenders pursuing guarantors through parallel Section 95 applications can now rely on Section 96(4) even where their own application long predates the amendment, provided it was still pending when the change took effect.
why_it_matters: Personal guarantees given by promoters and family businesses for company loans had, until this year, come with an unintended escape hatch: filing one Section 95 application triggered an automatic moratorium that shielded the guarantor from every other lender's recovery action. This ruling confirms that the 2026 amendment removing that shield applies even to applications filed before the amendment existed, so guarantors cannot rely on pre-amendment filings to resist parallel recovery by other creditors.
card_summary: NCLAT holds the 2026 IBC amendment excluding personal guarantors from the Section 96 interim moratorium applies retroactively, rejecting their plea that a pre-amendment filing should escape it.
card_tip: A personal guarantor cannot rely on an interim moratorium from a pre-amendment Section 95 filing to resist a lender's recovery action; Section 96(4) reaches pending cases regardless of filing date.
